content:
Over the past couple of days, two reports have appeared pointing to two different ways in which Apple is looking to boost its earnings by growing its services revenue.

In my view, it should absolutely do the first, but not the second – and it looks like Phil Schiller may agree …

First, a summary of the two reports.

Home security and monitoring service

On Friday, Bloomberg reported that Apple is planning to launch a brand-new home security and monitoring service, to be offered alongside some new home hardware we’ve been expecting.

Squeezing more revenue from the App Store

The same source published a second piece on Sunday, saying Apple is looking at ways to squeeze more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Apple shouldn’t do the latter

To take them in reverse order, I think the second approach would be a huge mistake.

Apple’s effective monopoly on iPhone app sales has come under attack from regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell an iPhone app, you have to do it through the official App Store, so you have no choice but to accept the company’s take-it-or-leave-it terms.

I get the general argument that nobody is forced to buy an iPhone or develop apps for it, but that’s not how even the most laissez-faire form of capitalism is supposed to work in practice: the US has had anti-monopoly laws since 1890 for exactly this reason. When you reach a certain level of market dominance, there are constraints, to ensure you don’t abuse your position.

Trying to squeeze more money from the App Store is exactly the opposite of ‘skating to where the puck is going,’ a view reportedly shared by Phil Schiller, which Bloomberg cites as one of the reasons for his stepping back now.

Innovative services are the right direction

By contrast, launching brand-new innovative services that people want to buy is exactly the right thing for Apple to be doing. I can easily see the value of the company offering a home security monitoring service.

I argued back in 2024 that making its own smart home cameras would be one of the … smartest things the company could do. I feel the same way about the rumored Apple smart doorbell. There are two solid reasons why it would make complete sense for security products to have an optional services component.

First, all the privacy arguments I’ve previously made. HomeKit Secure Video has already done a huge amount to ensure the privacy of security camera footage. If there’s one company I’d trust to do AI analysis of security camera footage, it’s Apple.

Second, Apple is of course best-placed to fully integrate security hardware and services within a HomeKit environment. I’m sure there are plenty of other areas in which Apple could offer similar benefits.

For me, the key thing is that Apple needs to take the same approach to services as it does to hardware: Make brilliant products that people are happy – even delighted – to pay for. Not try to squeeze money in ways that wind up customers, developers, and regulators.

What’s your view? Please share your thoughts in the comments.
